title: Angel Reese Takes Podcast Break After WNBA Season, Vows to Dedicate Off‑Season to Herself
body:
Angel Reese announced she will step away from her regular podcast appearances this offseason, choosing to focus exclusively on recovery and personal development after the Atlanta Dream’s hard‑fought run to the WNBA Finals. The 23‑year‑old forward, who helped propel the Dream to their first championship series in franchise history, said the grueling 40‑game schedule, combined with the physical toll of a full college‑to‑pro transition, has left her eager to prioritize health and self‑growth before the next campaign begins.

Reese’s decision comes on the heels of a season that saw the Dream surge from a middling regular‑season record to a dramatic upset over the top‑seeded Chicago Sky in the semifinals, only to fall short in a tightly contested five‑game series against the Las Vegas Aces. Throughout the playoffs, Reese logged an average of 14.2 points, 6.1 rebounds, and 3.4 assists per game, while also shouldering a heavy defensive load. The intensity of those performances, coupled with the added responsibility of being a media magnet after her viral “crossover queen” moment in college, has amplified the need for a deliberate break.

In a candid interview with her podcast co‑host, Reese explained that the offseason will be “all about me.” She plans to engage in a structured rehabilitation program designed by the Dream’s medical staff, focusing on strengthening her knees and lower back—areas that showed signs of strain during the championship series. Additionally, Reese intends to work with a sports psychologist to refine her mental resilience, a move that reflects a growing trend among elite athletes who recognize the importance of psychological well‑being alongside physical conditioning.

The move also signals a shift in how WNBA players manage their workloads. Historically, many athletes have filled the summer months with overseas contracts, overseas leagues, or continuous media engagements, often leading to burnout. Reese’s choice to forgo additional commitments underscores a broader conversation within the league about sustainable career paths. The WNBA Players Association has recently advocated for longer seasons and improved health benefits, and Reese’s public dedication to self‑care may encourage peers to consider similar pauses, potentially reshaping the off‑season culture.

From a team perspective, the Dream will need to adjust to Reese’s reduced media presence while still relying on her on‑court contributions. Head coach Tanisha Wright praised Reese’s professionalism, noting that “her commitment to coming back stronger benefits the whole locker room.” The coaching staff is already mapping out a conditioning plan that will integrate Reese’s rehab timeline with the team’s preseason schedule, ensuring she returns at peak performance for the 2025 campaign.

Looking ahead, Reese’s offseason strategy could pay dividends both personally and for the Dream’s championship aspirations. By entering the next season refreshed and physically optimized, she positions herself as a cornerstone of Atlanta’s bid to return to the Finals. Moreover, her openness about prioritizing mental health may inspire a new generation of athletes to view self‑care as a competitive advantage rather than a concession. As the WNBA continues to grow in visibility and revenue, Reese’s choice highlights the evolving balance between fame, performance, and personal well‑being—a balance that could define the league’s future trajectory.
